name: Iseult
one_line: Married to one man, bound to another by an accident with a cup, and the only lover in the canon with a defensible case.
dossier:
Iseult of Ireland is fetched across the sea to marry a man she has never met, and on the voyage she and her escort drink a potion her own mother brewed for the wedding night. From that point neither of them has a will in the matter.

The tradition is unusually kind to her as a result. Guinevere's affair is a choice and is judged as one; Iseult's is a chemical fact. Gottfried builds an entire poem on the distinction, and readers have argued ever since about whether it makes her innocent or merely doomed.

Malory keeps her as a courtly figure and gives her a rival with almost the same name — Iseult of the White Hands, whom Tristram marries and does not touch, which is its own small cruelty. She survives Tristram's murder and dies over his body.

arc.note: the cup, and everything after it

cost: She is the proof that removing the choice does not remove the ruin.
